label: lem:C-moments
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:C-moments}
The functions $\mathfrak{T}$ and $\mathfrak{S}$ are $C^\infty$ on $[0,\infty)\times[0,1]$, with one-sided
derivatives on the boundary, and so are
\[
 \mathfrak R(w,\theta)=\frac{\mathfrak{T}(w,\theta)}w,\qquad
 \mathfrak D(w,\theta)=\frac{\mathfrak{S}(w,\theta)-\mathfrak R(w,\theta)}w ,
\]
extended continuously to $w=0$. For every $\theta\in[0,1]$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C-jets}
 \mathfrak R(0,\theta)=1,\qquad \partial_w\mathfrak R(0,\theta)=\theta-2,\qquad
 \mathfrak D(0,\theta)=-\theta,\qquad
 \partial_w\mathfrak D(0,\theta)=\tfrac43+3\theta-\theta^2 .
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Gaussian jets

label: eq:C-heat-jets
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $g(x,\theta)$ be smooth on $\mathbb{R}\times[0,1]$ with
$|\partial_x^k\partial_\theta^jg(x,\theta)|\le C_{k,j}(1+|x|)^je^{|x|}$ for all $k,j\ge0$, and
put $M_g(w,\theta)=\mathbb{E} g(\sqrt wZ,\theta)$ with $Z$ standard Gaussian. For $w>0$, write $M_g$ as
the integral of $g$ against the $\mathcal N(0,w)$ density $\varphi_w$. Since
$\partial_w\varphi_w=\frac12\varphi_w''$, differentiation under the integral and two
integrations by parts give $\partial_wM_g=\frac12M_{\partial_x^2g}$; the boundary terms vanish
because $\varphi_w$ has Gaussian decay. The right side is continuous on
$[0,\infty)\times[0,1]$ by dominated convergence, so
$M_g(w,\theta)-M_g(0,\theta)=\frac12\int_0^wM_{\partial_x^2g}(s,\theta)\,ds$, and the identity
$\partial_wM_g=\frac12M_{\partial_x^2g}$ extends to $w=0$. Differentiation in $\theta$ under the
expectation is also dominated. Iterating, every mixed partial derivative of $M_g$ exists and is
continuous, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C-heat-jets}
 \partial_w^kM_g(0,\theta)=2^{-k}\,\partial_x^{2k}g(0,\theta)\qquad(k\ge0).
\end{equation}
The functions $\cosh^\theta x$, $\tanh^2x\cosh^\theta x$ and $\operatorname{sech}^4x\cosh^\theta x$ satisfy
the growth hypothesis: each $x$-derivative of $\cosh^\theta x$ is a polynomial in
$(\theta,\tanh x)$ times $\cosh^\theta x\le e^{|x|}$, and each $\theta$-derivative contributes a
factor $\log\cosh x$, which lies in $[0,|x|]$. Since $\mathbb{E}\cosh^\theta(\sqrt wZ)\ge1$, the
functions $\mathfrak{T}$ and $\mathfrak{S}$ are smooth quotients. Moreover $\mathfrak{T}(0,\theta)=0$ and
$\mathfrak{S}(0,\theta)=1$. Hence $\mathfrak R(w,\theta)=\int_0^1\partial_w\mathfrak{T}(sw,\theta)\,ds$ is
smooth, with $\mathfrak R(0,\theta)=\partial_w\mathfrak{T}(0,\theta)$, and the same representation
applies to $\mathfrak D$ once $\mathfrak{S}(0,\theta)=\mathfrak R(0,\theta)$ is checked below.

By \eqref{eq:C-heat-jets}, an even function with Taylor coefficients $g_0,g_2,g_4,g_6$ at
$x=0$ has $M_g(w)=g_0+g_2w+3g_4w^2+15g_6w^3+O(w^4)$ at fixed $\theta$. From
\begin{gather*}
 \log\cosh x=\tfrac{x^2}2-\tfrac{x^4}{12}+O(x^6),\qquad
 \tanh^2x=x^2-\tfrac23x^4+\tfrac{17}{45}x^6+O(x^8),\\
 \operatorname{sech}^4x=1-2x^2+\tfrac73x^4+O(x^6),
\end{gather*}
we get $\cosh^\theta x=1+\frac\theta2x^2+(\frac{\theta^2}8-\frac\theta{12})x^4+O(x^6)$, and
therefore
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{E}\cosh^\theta(\sqrt wZ)
 &=1+\tfrac\theta2\,w+\bigl(\tfrac{3\theta^2}8-\tfrac\theta4\bigr)w^2+O(w^3),\\
 \mathbb{E}\bigl[\tanh^2\cosh^\theta\bigr](\sqrt wZ)
 &=w+\bigl(\tfrac{3\theta}2-2\bigr)w^2
   +\bigl(\tfrac{15\theta^2}8-\tfrac{25\theta}4+\tfrac{17}3\bigr)w^3+O(w^4),\\
 \mathbb{E}\bigl[\operatorname{sech}^4\cosh^\theta\bigr](\sqrt wZ)
 &=1+\bigl(\tfrac\theta2-2\bigr)w+\bigl(\tfrac{3\theta^2}8-\tfrac{13\theta}4+7\bigr)w^2+O(w^3).
\end{align*}
Dividing by the first series,
\[
 \mathfrak{T}(w,\theta)=w+(\theta-2)w^2+\bigl(\theta^2-5\theta+\tfrac{17}3\bigr)w^3+O(w^4),\qquad
 \mathfrak{S}(w,\theta)=1-2w+(7-2\theta)w^2+O(w^3).
\]
Thus $\mathfrak R=1+(\theta-2)w+(\theta^2-5\theta+\frac{17}3)w^2+O(w^3)$, so
$\mathfrak{S}(0,\theta)=\mathfrak R(0,\theta)=1$, and
$\mathfrak D=-\theta+(\frac43+3\theta-\theta^2)w+O(w^2)$. All functions involved are smooth, so
these Taylor coefficients are the values in \eqref{eq:C-jets}.

title: Proof
body_md:
By the chain rule, each derivative in question is a polynomial with universal coefficients in
the derivatives of order at most two of $\mathfrak R$, $\mathfrak D$, $\mathfrak{S}$ at
$(\xi'(q),\theta)$ and in $\ell,\ell',\ell'',\chi,\chi',\chi'',\xi''(q),\xi'''(q)$. The former
are bounded by absolute constants on $[0,\frac12]\times[0,1]$, and the latter by
Lemma~\ref{lem:dat-class-bounds} with $\varepsilon=\frac14$. For the identities,
$\mathfrak{T}(\xi'(q),\theta)=\xi'(q)\mathfrak R(\xi'(q),\theta)=q\ell(q)\mathfrak R(\xi'(q),\theta)$,
and, with $\xi''=\ell+q\chi$ and $\mathfrak{S}-\mathfrak R=\xi'(q)\mathfrak D=q\ell\mathfrak D$,
\[
 \xi''\mathfrak{S}-\ell\mathfrak R=\ell(\mathfrak{S}-\mathfrak R)+q\chi\mathfrak{S}
 =q\bigl(\ell^2\mathfrak D+\chi\mathfrak{S}\bigr),
\]
where $\mathfrak{S}$, $\mathfrak R$, $\mathfrak D$ are evaluated at $(\xi'(q),\theta)$. The jets
follow from \eqref{eq:C-jets}, $\mathfrak{S}(0,\theta)=1$, $\frac{d}{dq}\xi'(q)=\xi''(q)$, and
$\ell(0)=a_0$, $\ell'(0)=0$, $\chi(0)=0$, $\chi'(0)=\xi''''(0)/3$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\xi\in\mathcal{K}(\frac14)$ with $\tau\le\tau_0$. Since $\tau_0\le\frac12K_{\rm rs}$, we have
$2\tau\le K_{\rm rs}$.

(a) By \eqref{eq:C-zero-jets}, $\partial_q\Upsilon(0,\theta)\le-a_0^2<-1$. Since the first
and second derivatives of $\Upsilon$ are bounded by $\overline C$ and
$K_{\rm rs}\le1/(2\overline C)$,
$-\overline C\le\partial_q\Upsilon\le-\frac12$ on $[0,K_{\rm rs}]\times[0,1]$. Hence
\[
 \tau-\overline Cq\le\Upsilon(q,\theta)\le\tau-\tfrac q2\qquad(0\le q\le K_{\rm rs}).
\]
Since $2\tau\le K_{\rm rs}$, the strictly decreasing function $\Upsilon(\cdot,\theta)$ has
exactly one zero in $(0,K_{\rm rs}]$, and it lies in $[\tau/\overline C,2\tau]$. By
\eqref{eq:C-rs-identity} this zero is the only solution $q^{\mathrm{rs}}_\theta$ of
$q=\mathfrak{T}(\xi'(q),\theta)$ in $(0,K_{\rm rs}]$. Since $\partial_q\Upsilon\ne0$, the implicit
function theorem and uniqueness make $\theta\mapstoq^{\mathrm{rs}}_\theta$ continuously differentiable,
with $dq^{\mathrm{rs}}_\theta/d\theta=-\partial_\theta\Upsilon/\partial_q\Upsilon$ at
$(q^{\mathrm{rs}}_\theta,\theta)$; at $\theta\in\{0,1\}$ the same formula for the one-sided derivative
follows from the mean value theorem on the convex set $[0,K_{\rm rs}]\times[0,1]$.

(b) At $q=q^{\mathrm{rs}}_\theta$, \eqref{eq:C-rs-identity} gives $\mathfrak{T}(\xi'(q),\theta)/q=1$, and
\eqref{eq:C-at-identity} gives
\[
 \mathfrak A(\theta)-1=q^{\mathrm{rs}}_\theta\,\mathfrak W(\theta),\qquad
 \mathfrak W(\theta)=\varpi(q^{\mathrm{rs}}_\theta,\theta).
\]
Since $q^{\mathrm{rs}}_\theta>0$, the sign of $\mathfrak A-1$ is the sign of $\mathfrak W$, and it suffices
to show that $\mathfrak W$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$ with
$\mathfrak W(0)>0>\mathfrak W(1)$. Because $\partial_\theta\Upsilon(0,\theta)=0$, we have
$|\partial_\theta\Upsilon(q,\theta)|\le\overline Cq$, hence
$|dq^{\mathrm{rs}}_\theta/d\theta|\le2\overline Cq^{\mathrm{rs}}_\theta\le4\overline C\tau$. Also
$\partial_\theta\varpi(q,\theta)\le-a_0^2+\overline Cq\le-1+2\overline C\tau$ at
$q=q^{\mathrm{rs}}_\theta$. Therefore
\[
 \frac{d\mathfrak W}{d\theta}
 =\partial_\theta\varpi+\partial_q\varpi\,\frac{dq^{\mathrm{rs}}_\theta}{d\theta}
 \le-1+2\overline C\tau+4\overline C^2\tau\le-\tfrac12 ,
\]
since $\tau\le1/(12\overline C^2)$ and $\overline C\ge1$. With $q^{\mathrm{rs}}_0\le2\tau$, Taylor's
formula at $(0,0)$ and \eqref{eq:C-zero-jets}, where $\varpi(0,0)=0$ and
$\partial_q\varpi(0,0)=\frac43a_0^3+\frac13\xi''''(0)\ge\frac43$, and the bound
$|\partial_q\varpi|\le\overline C$ with $q^{\mathrm{rs}}_1\le2\tau$ give
\[
 \mathfrak W(0)\ge\partial_q\varpi(0,0)\,q^{\mathrm{rs}}_0-\tfrac{\overline C}2\bigl(q^{\mathrm{rs}}_0\bigr)^2
 \geq^{\mathrm{rs}}_0\bigl(\tfrac43-\overline C\tau\bigr)>0,\qquad
 \mathfrak W(1)\le\varpi(0,1)+\overline Cq^{\mathrm{rs}}_1\le-1+2\overline C\tau<0 ;
\]
both signs hold because $\overline C\tau\le1/(12\overline C)\le\frac1{12}$. Hence $\mathfrak W$
has a unique zero $\theta_c\in(0,1)$, which is the threshold of~(b).

(c) Write $q_c=q^{\mathrm{rs}}_{\theta_c}\le2\tau$. Taylor's formula in $q$ at $(0,\theta_c)$, applied to
$\varpi(q_c,\theta_c)=\mathfrak W(\theta_c)=0$ and to $\Upsilon(q_c,\theta_c)=0$, gives by
\eqref{eq:C-zero-jets}
\[
 a_0^2\theta_c
 =\Bigl[a_0^3\bigl(\tfrac43+3\theta_c-\theta_c^2\bigr)+\tfrac13\xi''''(0)\Bigr]q_c+R_1,
 \qquad
 a_0^2(2-\theta_c)\,q_c=\tau+R_2,
\]
with $|R_1|,|R_2|\le\frac12\overline Cq_c^2\le2\overline C\tau^2$. Since $a_0\le\frac54$ and
$\xi''''(0)\le\frac14$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:dat-class-bounds}(i),(ii) with $\varepsilon=\frac14$),
the first identity gives $\theta_c\le C_1\tau$. As $a_0^2=(1+\tau)^2$, the second then gives
$|q_c-\frac\tau2|\le C_2\tau^2$. Substituting both into the first identity, every term other
than $(\frac43+\frac13\xi''''(0))q_c$ is at most $C_3\tau^2$. The constants $C_1,C_2,C_3$ are
absolute. Hence
$\theta_c=(\frac43+\frac13\xi''''(0))\frac\tau2+O(\tau^2)
=\frac23(1+\frac14\xi''''(0))\tau+O(\tau^2)$, with an absolute implied constant $C$.

title: Proof
body_md:
By \ref{item:dat-C4}, $\zeta\in\mathcal W$, and by \ref{item:dat-C1}, $r\le2\tau<K$. We use
three facts. First, $h<0$ on $[K,1]$, by \eqref{eq:nc-confinement}, which holds for every
measure in $\mathcal W$ (item~\ref{item:nc-positive} of the choice of constants in
Section~\ref{sec:nc-reference}). Second, $h(0)=0$, since $\Gamma^{\theta,r}(0)=0$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:plat-ito}(a)). Third, the intervals $(0,r)$ and $(r,K)$ are plateaus of $\zeta$,
of heights $\theta$ and $1$, contained in $(0,K)$. By \eqref{eq:nc-positive-third}, which also
holds for every measure in $\mathcal W$, $h'''=(\Gamma^{\theta,r})'''\ge2$ on each of them.
Since $h'$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, it is strictly convex on $[0,r]$ and on $[r,K]$.

\emph{The sign of $h$ on $(0,r)$.} The set $\mathcal L=\{t\in[0,r]:h'(t)\le0\}$ is a closed
interval containing $r$, because $h'$ is convex and continuous and $h'(r)\le0$. If
$\mathcal L=[0,r]$, then $\int_0^rh'=h(r)-h(0)=0$ would force $h'\equiv0$ on $[0,r]$, which is
impossible for a strictly convex function. Thus $\mathcal L=[s,r]$ with $s>0$, and $h'>0$ on
$[0,s)$, so $h>0$ on $(0,s]$. Moreover $s<r$, since otherwise $h'>0$ on $[0,r)$ would give
$h(r)>h(0)=0$. On $(s,r)$ strict convexity gives $h'<\max\{h'(s),h'(r)\}\le0$, so $h$ decreases
strictly on $[s,r]$ to $h(r)=0$, and $h>0$ on $[s,r)$. Hence $h>0$ on $(0,r)$.

\emph{The sign of $h$ on $(r,1]$.} We first show that $h'<0$ on some interval $(r,r+\delta)$.
This is immediate if $h'(r)<0$. If $h'(r)=0$, then $(\Gamma^{\theta,r})'(r)=1$, and
\eqref{eq:C-right-second} with $\Gamma^{\theta,r}(r)=r\le\frac1{20}$, $\xi''\ge1$ and
$\xi'''(r)\le\varepsilon_*r<\frac14$ (by \ref{item:dat-C1} and \ref{item:dat-C3}) gives
\[
 h''(r+)=(\Gamma^{\theta,r})''(r+)\le\xi'''(r)+\xi''(r)^2\Bigl(\frac{10}{20}-2\Bigr)
 <\frac14-\frac32<0 .
\]
The set $\mathcal L'=\{t\in[r,K]:h'(t)\le0\}$ is therefore a closed interval $[r,s']$ with
$s'>r$. Strict convexity gives $h'<0$ on $(r,s')$, so $h<0$ on $(r,s']$. If $s'<K$, then $h'>0$
on $(s',K]$ and $h(K)<0$ by the first fact, so $h<0$ on $(s',K]$ as well. Together with the
first fact, $h<0$ on $(r,1]$.

\emph{The obstacle.} By \eqref{eq:intro-obstacle},
\[
 \mathcal{O}_\zeta(t)-\mathcal{O}_\zeta(r)=\frac12\int_t^r\xi''(u)h(u)\,du\quad(t<r),\qquad
 \mathcal{O}_\zeta(t)-\mathcal{O}_\zeta(r)=-\frac12\int_r^t\xi''(u)h(u)\,du\quad(t>r),
\]
and both are positive by the signs of $h$ just proved. So $\mathcal{O}_\zeta$ has its strict minimum
over $[0,1]$ at $r$.

\emph{Minimality.} Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on $[0,1]$ with $\nu(\{0\})\ge\theta$.
Since $\mathcal{O}_\zeta\ge\mathcal{O}_\zeta(r)$ and $\mathcal{O}_\zeta(0)-\mathcal{O}_\zeta(r)>0$,
\[
 \int\mathcal{O}_\zeta\,d\nu
 \ge\mathcal{O}_\zeta(r)+\nu(\{0\})\bigl(\mathcal{O}_\zeta(0)-\mathcal{O}_\zeta(r)\bigr)
 \ge\mathcal{O}_\zeta(r)+\theta\bigl(\mathcal{O}_\zeta(0)-\mathcal{O}_\zeta(r)\bigr)
 =\int\mathcal{O}_\zeta\,d\zeta .
\]
The segment $s\mapsto(1-s)\zeta+s\nu$ stays in the constrained set. Along it the Parisi
functional is convex, and its right derivative at $s=0$ is $\int\mathcal{O}_\zeta\,d(\nu-\zeta)$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:cons-standard}(c),(d); for this mixing direction the formula is also
\cite[Lemma~3.2 and Example~3.4]{JT17}). Convexity gives
\[
 P_\nu-P_\zeta\ge\int\mathcal{O}_\zeta\,d(\nu-\zeta)\ge0 .
\]
Thus $\zeta$ minimizes $P$ under the constraint $\zeta(\{0\})\ge\theta$, and the uniqueness in
Lemma~\ref{lem:cons-variational}(a) gives $\zeta_\theta=\zeta$. The positive contact set of
$\zeta_\theta$, the set of minimizers of $\mathcal{O}_{\zeta_\theta}$ over $(0,1]$, is $\{r\}$.

label: lem:D-support-relation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:D-support-relation}
Let $0<\theta<\theta_0$. Then $\alpha_\theta=R_{\zeta_\theta}$ on $(q_\theta,v_\theta)$ and
$\alpha_*=R_{\zeta_*}$ on $(0,v_*)$. Moreover $\alpha_\theta=\theta$ on $[0,q_\theta)$,
$\alpha_\theta=1$ on $[v_\theta,1]$ and $\alpha_*=1$ on $[v_*,1]$. Consequently $\alpha_*$ is
continuous on $[0,v_*)$ with $\alpha_*(t)\le C_0t$ there, $\alpha_\theta$ is continuous on
$(q_\theta,v_\theta)$ and right continuous at $q_\theta$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:D-alpha-star-linear}
 \alpha_*(t)=\rho_* t+O(t^2)\qquad(t\downarrow0),\qquad
 \rho_*=\frac{D_*}{2\sqrta_0} .
\end{equation}
Finally, for all small $\theta>0$, $\theta/C\le q_\theta\le C\theta$ and $|\Delta_\theta|\le
C\theta$ on $[0,q_\theta)$.
head: environment
name: Relations on the supports

title: Proof
body_md:
By \ref{item:D-F2}, $\Gamma_\theta(t)=t$ on $[q_\theta,v_\theta]$, so
$\Gamma_\theta'\equiv1$ on $(q_\theta,v_\theta)$, and both one-sided derivatives of
$\Gamma_\theta'$ vanish there. By Lemma~\ref{lem:plat-ito}(b) they equal
$N_{\zeta_\theta}(t)-\alpha_\theta(t)\sigma_{\zeta_\theta}(t)$ and
$N_{\zeta_\theta}(t)-\alpha_\theta(t-)\sigma_{\zeta_\theta}(t)$; since
$\sigma_{\zeta_\theta}\ge1$ \eqref{eq:D-rho-sigma}, $\alpha_\theta(t-)=\alpha_\theta(t)=
R_{\zeta_\theta}(t)$. The same argument applies to $\zeta_*$ on $(0,v_*)$, because $\Gamma_*$
is the identity on $[0,v_*]$ by \ref{item:D-F1}. The values on the plateaus follow from
$\zeta_\theta(\{0\})=\theta$, $\zeta_\theta((0,q_\theta))=0$ and the supports. Expectations
along the diffusion of polynomials in the jets are continuous in time
(Section~\ref{sec:plat}), so $R_\zeta$ is continuous on $[0,K]$. Hence $\alpha_*$ is
continuous on $(0,v_*)$, and at zero because $\alpha_*(0)=\zeta_*(\{0\})=0$ and
$0\le\alpha_*=R_{\zeta_*}\le C_0t$ on $(0,v_*)$ by \eqref{eq:D-rho-sigma}. Likewise $\alpha_\theta$
is continuous on $(q_\theta,v_\theta)$ and right continuous at $q_\theta$.

For \eqref{eq:D-alpha-star-linear}, write $X=X^{\zeta_*}$. By evenness, (U1) and
\eqref{eq:D-moments}, $|U^*(t,x)-U_*|\le C_0(x^2+t)$, so $\mathbb{E} U^*(t,X_t)^2=U_*^2+O(t)$ and
$\mathbb{E} U^*(t,X_t)^3=U_*^3+O(t)$. Since $V^*(t,\cdot)$ is odd with $\partial_xV^*=W^*$,
$V^*(t,x)=W^*(t,0)x+O(|x|^3)$ and $W^*(t,0)=W_*+O(t)$, so
$\mathbb{E} V^*(t,X_t)^2=a_0W_*^2t+O(t^2)$ by \eqref{eq:D-moments}. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:dat-class-bounds}(iii), $a'(t)=\xi''''(0)\,t+O(t^2)$, and $a(t)=a_0+O(t^2)$
by Lemma~\ref{lem:dat-class-bounds}(ii). Hence
\[
 N_{\zeta_*}(t)=\bigl(\xi''''(0)U_*^2+a_0^3W_*^2\bigr)t+O(t^2)=D_* t+O(t^2),
 \qquad
 \sigma_{\zeta_*}(t)=2a_0^2U_*^3+O(t)=2\sqrta_0+O(t),
\]
using $U_*=a_0^{-1/2}$, and \eqref{eq:D-alpha-star-linear} follows from
$\alpha_*=N_{\zeta_*}/\sigma_{\zeta_*}$. The bounds on $q_\theta$ follow from \ref{item:D-F3}.
On $[0,q_\theta)$ we have $\Delta_\theta=\theta-\alpha_*$ and $0\le\alpha_*\le C_0q_\theta$, so
$|\Delta_\theta|\le\theta+C_0q_\theta\le C\theta$.

label: lem:D-plateau
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: The plateau acts through its first moment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply \eqref{eq:D-duality} with $\zeta=\zeta_*$, $\tilde\zeta=\zeta_\theta$, $t_1=q$ and $F=H$,
and let $\psi$ be the corresponding function. On $[0,q)$ the drifts differ by
\[
 \omega^{\zeta_\theta}-\omega^{\zeta_*}
 =a\bigl[\Delta_\theta\,u^\theta+\alpha_*\,(u^\theta-u^*)\bigr],
\]
and we treat the two terms separately; write $X=X^{\zeta_\theta}$ and
$\mathsf m_k(s)=\mathbb{E} X_s^k$.

\emph{The second term.} For $s<q$ we have $\alpha_*(s)\le C_0s$ and
$\int_s^1|\Delta_\theta|\le C\theta q+L_\theta$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:D-support-relation}. By
\eqref{eq:D-odd-stability}, $|\psi_x(s,x)|\le C_0|x|$ and \eqref{eq:D-moments}, this term
contributes at most $C\int_0^qs^2(\theta q+L_\theta)\,ds\le C(\theta^5+\theta^3L_\theta)$.

\emph{The first term.} It equals $\int_0^q\Delta_\theta(s)\,g(s)\,ds$ with
$g(s)=\mathbb{E}[a(s)\,u^\theta(s,X_s)\,\psi_x(s,X_s)]$. Put $\psi_j(s)=\partial_x^j\psi(s,0)$. The
function $x\mapsto u^\theta(s,x)\psi_x(s,x)$ is even, with sixth derivative bounded by $C_0$ by
(U1) and (U4), and its Taylor expansion at zero has the coefficients
$U^\theta(s,0)\psi_2(s)$ of $x^2$ and $\frac16(U^\theta(s,0)\psi_4(s)+W^\theta(s,0)\psi_2(s))$
of $x^4$. Since $\mathsf m_6(s)\le C_0s^3$,
\[
 g(s)=a(s)\Bigl[U^\theta(s,0)\,\psi_2(s)\,\mathsf m_2(s)
 +\tfrac16\bigl(U^\theta(s,0)\psi_4(s)+W^\theta(s,0)\psi_2(s)\bigr)\mathsf m_4(s)\Bigr]+O(s^3).
\]
To evaluate $\psi_2$, differentiate the backward equation twice in $x$ and set $x=0$. Since
$\psi_x(s,0)=\omega^{\zeta_*}(s,0)=\partial_x^2\omega^{\zeta_*}(s,0)=0$ by parity,
$\psi_2'(s)=-2\,\partial_x\omega^{\zeta_*}(s,0)\,\psi_2(s)-\frac{a(s)}2\,\psi_4(s)$,
where $0\le\partial_x\omega^{\zeta_*}(s,0)=a(s)\alpha_*(s)U^*(s,0)\le C_0s$. With $\psi_2(q)=H''(0)$,
$\psi_4(s)=H''''(0)+O(q-s)$ by (U4), and $a(s)=a_0+O(s)$, integration from $s$ to $q$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:D-psi-two}
 \psi_2(s)=H''(0)+\tfrac{a_0}2\,H''''(0)\,(q-s)+O(q^2)\qquad(0\le s\le q).
\end{equation}
Now insert \eqref{eq:D-psi-two}, $U^\theta(s,0)=U^\theta(0,0)+O(s)$,
$W^\theta(s,0)=W^\theta(0,0)+O(s)$ (by (U1)), $\psi_4=H''''(0)+O(q)$, $\psi_2=H''(0)+O(q)$,
$a(s)=a_0+O(s)$, $\mathsf m_2(s)=a_0 s+O(s^2)$ and $\mathsf m_4(s)=3a_0^2s^2+O(s^3)$
\eqref{eq:D-moments}. In the first summand of $g$ we keep
$a(s)U^\theta(s,0)\mathsf m_2(s)H''(0)$ exactly; the rest of that summand is
$\frac12a_0^3U^\theta(0,0)H''''(0)(q-s)s+O(qs^2+q^2s)$. The second summand equals
$\frac12a_0^3\bigl(U^\theta(0,0)H''''(0)+W^\theta(0,0)H''(0)\bigr)s^2+O(s^3+qs^2)$. The two
$H''''(0)$ contributions add up to $\gamma_\theta H''''(0)\bigl[(q-s)s+s^2\bigr]
=\gamma_\theta\,q\,H''''(0)\,s$, so
\[
 g(s)=H''(0)\,k_\theta(s)+\gamma_\theta\,q\,H''''(0)\,s+O\bigl(s^3+qs^2+q^2s\bigr).
\]
The cancellation of the terms in $s^2H''''(0)$ is the Gaussian effect described in
Section~\ref{sec:nc-stability}: at this order the plateau moves the law of $X_q$ only through
its variance. Multiplying by $\Delta_\theta$, which satisfies $|\Delta_\theta|\le C\theta$ on
$[0,q)$, and integrating leaves an error at most $C\theta q^4\le C\theta^5$. This proves
\eqref{eq:D-plateau}. Finally $a(s)=a_0+O(s)$, $U^\theta(s,0)=U^\theta(0,0)+O(s)$ and
$\mathsf m_2(s)=a_0 s+O(s^2)$ give $k_\theta(s)=a_0^2U^\theta(0,0)\,s+O(s^2)$, hence
$|\Pi_\theta-a_0^2U^\theta(0,0)I_\theta|\le C\theta\int_0^qs^2\,ds\le C\theta^4$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:D-contact-closure}
For all small $\theta>0$,
\[
 |I_\theta|\le C\bigl(\theta^4+\theta L_\theta\bigr),\qquad

name: Closure by the common contact

title: Proof
body_md:
For small $\theta$ we have $q<v_*$, so $q$ is a contact of both measures:
$\Gamma_\theta(q)=q=\Gamma_*(q)$ by \ref{item:D-F1} and \ref{item:D-F2}.
Test with $H_q=u^*(q,\cdot)^2$. It is
even, $\|H_q\|_{10}\le C_0$ by (U1), $H_q''(0)=2U^*(q,0)^2\in[2(1-\eta)^2,2]$ by
\ref{item:D-K2}, and $|H_q''''(0)|=8|U^*(q,0)W^*(q,0)|\le C_0$. Since
$\Gamma_\zeta(q)=\nu^\zeta_q\bigl(u^\zeta(q,\cdot)^2\bigr)$, the two contact identities give
\[
 \nu^\theta_q(H_q)-\nu^*_q(H_q)
 =\nu^\theta_q\bigl(u^*(q,\cdot)^2-u^\theta(q,\cdot)^2\bigr),
\]
and by \eqref{eq:D-odd-stability}, with $\int_q^1|\Delta_\theta|=L_\theta$, its absolute value is
at most $C_0L_\theta\,\mathbb{E}(X^{\zeta_\theta}_q)^2\le C_0qL_\theta$. Lemma~\ref{lem:D-plateau}
applied to $H_q/C_0$, followed by its second assertion, gives
\[
 \bigl[H_q''(0)\,a_0^2U^\theta(0,0)+\gamma_\theta\,q\,H_q''''(0)\bigr]\,I_\theta
 =O\bigl(\theta^4+\theta L_\theta\bigr).
\]
By \ref{item:D-K2} and \ref{item:D-K3} the bracket is at least $2(1-\eta)^3-C_0q\ge1$ for
small $\theta$, which gives the bound on $I_\theta$. Returning to \eqref{eq:D-plateau} for
$H_q$ gives $H_q''(0)\,|\Pi_\theta|\le C(qL_\theta+\theta^5+\theta^3L_\theta)+Cq|I_\theta|$,
which is the bound on $\Pi_\theta$. The last assertion is \eqref{eq:D-plateau} with these two
bounds.

name: Laws above the first contact

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply \eqref{eq:D-duality} with $\zeta=\zeta_*$, $\tilde\zeta=\zeta_\theta$ and $t_1=t$, and
split the integral at $q$. By the Markov property, the part over $[0,q]$ is the right side of
\eqref{eq:D-duality} for $t_1=q$ and the test function $H=\psi(q,\cdot)$, so it equals
